topics.description: A named identity the system uses to control what a person or service may do. Each has a numeric UID; the name is for humans, the UID is what the kernel enforces on.
topics.notes: Depth rationale: command-bearing: the exam can ask which command or option fits a stated need.

topics.description: A named collection of users, used to grant a permission once to many accounts instead of repeating it per user.
topics.notes: Depth rationale: command-bearing: the exam can ask which command or option fits a stated need.

topics.description: The numeric user and group identifiers the kernel actually checks. UID 0 is root, and it is the number rather than the name "root" that confers privilege.
topics.notes: Depth rationale: command-bearing: the exam can ask which command or option fits a stated need.

topics.description: A user has exactly one primary group, applied to files they create, plus any number of supplementary groups that add access.
topics.notes: usermod -G without -a silently replaces every supplementary group; a classic destructive mistake. Depth rationale: command-bearing: the exam can ask which command or option fits a stated need.

topics.description: World-readable account database with seven colon-separated fields: username, password placeholder (x), UID, GID, comment/GECOS, home directory, login shell. Despite the name it no longer holds passwords — the placeholder points at /etc/shadow.
topics.notes: Field count and order are standard recall items; the password placeholder is easy to forget when counting. Depth rationale: command-bearing: the exam can ask which command or option fits a stated need.

topics.description: Holds password hashes and ageing policy, and is never world-readable — which is why hashes moved here out of /etc/passwd. Exact permissions are distribution-specific: Debian-family systems ship it 0640 root:shadow, so the shadow group can read it, while Red Hat-family systems ship it 0000 root:root.
topics.notes: Depth rationale: command-bearing: the exam can ask which command or option fits a stated need.

topics.description: Group database with four colon-separated fields: group name, password placeholder, GID, and the comma-separated supplementary member list.
topics.notes: Depth rationale: command-bearing: the exam can ask which command or option fits a stated need.

topics.description: The program started when a user logs in. Setting it to /usr/sbin/nologin is the standard way to create an account that owns files but cannot log in.
topics.notes: Depth rationale: command-bearing: the exam can ask which command or option fits a stated need.

topics.description: An unprivileged account that exists to run a daemon rather than to be logged into, limiting the damage a compromised service can do.
topics.notes: Depth rationale: either end of a named confusable pair, which is exactly the shape a multiple-choice comparison question takes.

topics.description: Rules governing password expiry, minimum age, and warning periods, enforced from /etc/shadow fields.
topics.notes: Depth rationale: command-bearing: the exam can ask which command or option fits a stated need.

topics.description: The three permission bits. On a directory they mean something different from a file: execute means "may traverse into", and write means "may create or delete entries".
topics.notes: The directory semantics are the most commonly missed part of this topic. Depth rationale: command-bearing: the exam can ask which command or option fits a stated need.

topics.description: The three permission classes. The kernel checks them in order and stops at the first match, so a more permissive "other" cannot rescue a restrictive "group".
topics.notes: First-match-wins is counter-intuitive and is a classic exam distinction. Depth rationale: command-bearing: the exam can ask which command or option fits a stated need.

topics.description: Two notations for the same thing: u+x style symbolic changes are relative; 755 style octal is absolute and replaces all bits.
topics.notes: Depth rationale: specific configuration syntax is itself examinable.

topics.description: Change the owning user and owning group of a file. Only root can give a file away to another user.
topics.notes: Depth rationale: command-bearing: the exam can ask which command or option fits a stated need.

topics.description: A mask of bits removed from the default permissions of newly created files. It subtracts; it does not set.
topics.notes: Frequently confused with chmod because both use octal. Depth rationale: command-bearing: the exam can ask which command or option fits a stated need.

topics.description: Runs an executable with the file owner’s privileges rather than the caller’s. This is how passwd lets an ordinary user write to /etc/shadow.
topics.notes: Depth rationale: command-bearing: the exam can ask which command or option fits a stated need.

topics.description: On a binary, runs with the group’s privileges. On a directory, makes new files inherit the directory’s group — the usual way to build a shared team folder.
topics.notes: Depth rationale: command-bearing: the exam can ask which command or option fits a stated need.

topics.description: On a shared-writable directory, restricts deletion and renaming of a file to the file's owner, the directory's owner, or a privileged process. This is why /tmp is world-writable yet users cannot delete each other's files.
topics.notes: Depth rationale: command-bearing: the exam can ask which command or option fits a stated need.

topics.description: Root bypasses permission checks entirely. The operating principle is to grant the minimum privilege sufficient for the task rather than working as root.
topics.notes: Depth rationale: either end of a named confusable pair, which is exactly the shape a multiple-choice comparison question takes.

topics.description: sudo runs a single command as another user under a policy and logs it; su starts a whole shell as that user and requires the target account’s password.
topics.notes: The auditability difference is the point, not the convenience. Depth rationale: command-bearing: the exam can ask which command or option fits a stated need.

topics.description: The sudo policy file, edited via visudo so a syntax error cannot lock everyone out.
topics.notes: Editing sudoers directly with a text editor is the mistake visudo exists to prevent. Depth rationale: specific configuration syntax is itself examinable.

topics.description: A running instance of a program, with its own PID, memory, and open files.
topics.notes: Depth rationale: command-bearing: the exam can ask which command or option fits a stated need.

topics.description: The process identifier and its parent’s. PID 1 is the init system and is the ancestor of everything else.
topics.notes: Depth rationale: command-bearing: the exam can ask which command or option fits a stated need.

topics.description: Shell job control: & starts a job in the background, Ctrl-Z suspends, bg and fg move jobs between states.
topics.notes: Depth rationale: command-bearing: the exam can ask which command or option fits a stated need.

topics.description: Asynchronous notifications sent to processes. SIGTERM asks politely and can be caught; SIGKILL cannot be caught and gives no chance to clean up.
topics.notes: Reaching for kill -9 first is the classic beginner error. Depth rationale: command-bearing: the exam can ask which command or option fits a stated need.

topics.description: The nice value biases CPU scheduling, from -20 (greediest) to 19. Raising your own niceness is always allowed; lowering it requires root or CAP_SYS_NICE unless the administrator has raised RLIMIT_NICE, which defaults to no allowance.
topics.notes: Depth rationale: command-bearing: the exam can ask which command or option fits a stated need.

topics.description: A long-running background process, usually started at boot and not attached to a terminal.
topics.notes: Depth rationale: either end of a named confusable pair, which is exactly the shape a multiple-choice comparison question takes.

topics.description: A zombie has exited but its parent has not reaped its status; an orphan’s parent died and it is re-parented to PID 1.
topics.notes: Depth rationale: peripheral or specialist for an entry-level exam; recognition of the term is sufficient.

topics.description: A managed, usually long-running facility the system starts, stops, and supervises — as opposed to a bare process you launch by hand.
topics.notes: process vs service is one of the named comparisons an LFCA candidate should be able to make. Depth rationale: command-bearing: the exam can ask which command or option fits a stated need.

topics.description: The init system and service manager on most modern distributions. Runs as PID 1 and supervises everything else.
topics.notes: Depth rationale: command-bearing: the exam can ask which command or option fits a stated need.

topics.description: systemd’s unit of management. Types include .service, .socket, .timer, .mount, and .target; the unit file declares how it behaves.
topics.notes: Depth rationale: command-bearing: the exam can ask which command or option fits a stated need.

topics.description: start affects the running system now; enable affects whether it comes up at boot. Neither implies the other.
topics.notes: A very commonly tested distinction, and a common real-world outage cause. Depth rationale: specific configuration syntax is itself examinable.

topics.description: A grouping of units representing a system state, the modern replacement for the older runlevel concept.
topics.notes: Depth rationale: command-bearing: the exam can ask which command or option fits a stated need.

topics.description: The older SysV notion of system state (0 halt, 1 single-user, 3 multi-user, 5 graphical, 6 reboot), now mapped onto systemd targets.
topics.notes: Depth rationale: command-bearing: the exam can ask which command or option fits a stated need.

topics.description: Tells systemd to re-read unit files after they change. Editing a unit without it leaves systemd acting on the old definition.
topics.notes: Depth rationale: command-bearing: the exam can ask which command or option fits a stated need.

topics.description: A distributable archive bundling software with its metadata, dependency list, and install scripts.
topics.notes: Depth rationale: either end of a named confusable pair, which is exactly the shape a multiple-choice comparison question takes.

topics.description: A server-hosted collection of packages the package manager can search and install from.
topics.notes: package vs repository is a named comparison for this exam. Depth rationale: either end of a named confusable pair, which is exactly the shape a multiple-choice comparison question takes.

topics.description: A package another package requires. The manager resolves these automatically; a broken dependency tree is a common failure symptom.
topics.notes: Depth rationale: conceptual: explain what it is and why it exists.

topics.description: dpkg installs a single local .deb and does not resolve dependencies; apt works with repositories and does.
topics.notes: Depth rationale: command-bearing: the exam can ask which command or option fits a stated need.

topics.description: The Red Hat equivalents: rpm handles a single local package, dnf (formerly yum) handles repositories and dependencies.
topics.notes: Depth rationale: command-bearing: the exam can ask which command or option fits a stated need.

topics.description: On Debian systems apt update only refreshes the package index; apt upgrade actually installs newer versions. The names mislead.
topics.notes: A frequent point of confusion worth knowing precisely. Depth rationale: command-bearing: the exam can ask which command or option fits a stated need.

topics.description: The disciplined practice of tracking, testing, and applying updates — particularly security updates — on a schedule rather than ad hoc.
topics.notes: Depth rationale: either end of a named confusable pair, which is exactly the shape a multiple-choice comparison question takes.

topics.description: The convention defining what lives where on a Linux system, which is what makes /etc mean the same thing across distributions.
topics.notes: Depth rationale: either end of a named confusable pair, which is exactly the shape a multiple-choice comparison question takes.

topics.description: System-wide configuration files. Host-specific and, by convention, text.
topics.notes: Depth rationale: conceptual: explain what it is and why it exists.

topics.description: Variable data that grows at runtime: logs, spools, caches. A full /var is a very common cause of service failure.
topics.notes: Depth rationale: conceptual: explain what it is and why it exists.

topics.description: The directory beneath which regular users' personal home directories usually live (for example /home/alice), each serving as that user's default working directory and $HOME at login; hier(7) notes the exact structure beneath /home is a local administration decision. The superuser's home directory, /root, is a separate, optional directory kept outside /home — the FHS's stated rationale is that if root's home directory were not stored on the root partition, the system would need a fallback default in case that location could not be found, exactly the risk /home carries when it is mounted from a separate partition that fails to come up. Assuming root's home is /home/root, rather than /root, is the recurring mistake.
topics.notes: Depth rationale: conceptual: explain what it is and why it exists.

topics.description: Read-only user-land programs and libraries installed by the distribution.
topics.notes: Depth rationale: conceptual: explain what it is and why it exists.

topics.description: World-writable temporary space, typically cleared on reboot and protected by the sticky bit.
topics.notes: Depth rationale: conceptual: explain what it is and why it exists.

topics.description: Virtual filesystems exposing kernel and process state as files rather than occupying disk.
topics.notes: Depth rationale: command-bearing: the exam can ask which command or option fits a stated need.

topics.description: Device nodes representing hardware and pseudo-devices such as /dev/null.
topics.notes: Depth rationale: either end of a named confusable pair, which is exactly the shape a multiple-choice comparison question takes.

topics.description: The on-disk format — ext4, XFS, Btrfs, vFAT, NTFS — determining features such as journaling and maximum file size.
topics.notes: Depth rationale: command-bearing: the exam can ask which command or option fits a stated need.

topics.description: Attaching a filesystem into the single unified directory tree at a mount point, rather than exposing it as a separate drive letter.
topics.notes: Depth rationale: command-bearing: the exam can ask which command or option fits a stated need.

topics.description: Declares which filesystems mount where at boot, and with what options.
topics.notes: A malformed entry can prevent a machine from booting. Depth rationale: command-bearing: the exam can ask which command or option fits a stated need.

topics.description: A subdivision of a block device, which then holds a filesystem.
topics.notes: Depth rationale: command-bearing: the exam can ask which command or option fits a stated need.

topics.description: The structure holding a file’s metadata and block pointers. A filesystem can exhaust inodes while still showing free space.
topics.notes: The "disk full but df shows space" scenario is an inode exhaustion classic. Depth rationale: command-bearing: the exam can ask which command or option fits a stated need.

topics.description: A hard link is another name for the same inode; a symlink is a small file pointing at a path and can dangle if the target moves.
topics.notes: Depth rationale: command-bearing: the exam can ask which command or option fits a stated need.

topics.description: df reports per-filesystem free space; du walks a directory tree adding up file sizes. They routinely disagree, and the reason matters.
topics.notes: A deleted-but-still-open file is the usual explanation for the discrepancy. Depth rationale: diagnostic: the exam can present symptoms and ask for the cause or the first check.

topics.description: Disk space used to extend memory under pressure. Heavy swapping is a symptom of memory shortage, not a solution to it.
topics.notes: Depth rationale: command-bearing: the exam can ask which command or option fits a stated need.

topics.description: Logical Volume Management: an abstraction over physical devices allowing volumes to be resized and spanned. Recognition-level for LFCA.
topics.notes: Depth rationale: peripheral or specialist for an entry-level exam; recognition of the term is sufficient.

topics.description: Combining disks for redundancy or speed: RAID 0 stripes with no redundancy, 1 mirrors, 5 uses parity, 10 mirrors and stripes.
topics.notes: RAID is not a backup — it protects against drive failure, not deletion or corruption. Depth rationale: either end of a named confusable pair, which is exactly the shape a multiple-choice comparison question takes.

topics.description: The traditional time-based job scheduler, configured per user via crontab or system-wide in /etc/cron.d.
topics.notes: Depth rationale: command-bearing: the exam can ask which command or option fits a stated need.

topics.description: Five time fields — minute, hour, day of month, month, day of week — then the command. Cron jobs run with a minimal environment and a different PATH from your shell.
topics.notes: The sparse environment is the usual reason a script works interactively but fails under cron. Depth rationale: specific configuration syntax is itself examinable.

topics.description: The systemd alternative to cron, with logging through the journal, dependency handling, and the ability to catch up on missed runs.
topics.notes: Depth rationale: command-bearing: the exam can ask which command or option fits a stated need.

topics.description: The conventional location for plain-text log files.
topics.notes: Depth rationale: command-bearing: the exam can ask which command or option fits a stated need.

topics.description: The traditional logging protocol and its severity scale from emergency down to debug, used for filtering.
topics.notes: Depth rationale: either end of a named confusable pair, which is exactly the shape a multiple-choice comparison question takes.

topics.description: systemd’s structured, binary, queryable log store, read with journalctl rather than a pager.
topics.notes: Depth rationale: diagnostic: the exam can present symptoms and ask for the cause or the first check.

topics.description: Rotating, compressing, and expiring logs so they cannot fill the disk.
topics.notes: Depth rationale: command-bearing: the exam can ask which command or option fits a stated need.

topics.description: Firmware, then bootloader, then kernel, then the init system, then services — knowing the order is what makes boot failures diagnosable.
topics.notes: Depth rationale: command-bearing: the exam can ask which command or option fits a stated need.

topics.description: The two firmware generations. UEFI adds an EFI system partition, GPT partitioning, larger disk support, and Secure Boot.
topics.notes: Depth rationale: either end of a named confusable pair, which is exactly the shape a multiple-choice comparison question takes.

topics.description: The stage that loads the kernel and passes it parameters. GRUB is the common Linux implementation.
topics.notes: Depth rationale: command-bearing: the exam can ask which command or option fits a stated need.

topics.description: The core of the operating system: it mediates access to CPU, memory, devices, and enforces permissions.
topics.notes: Depth rationale: command-bearing: the exam can ask which command or option fits a stated need.

topics.description: Recording what a system does, why it was configured that way, and how to recover it. Undocumented systems fail badly precisely when the person who built them is unavailable.
topics.notes: Depth rationale: either end of a named confusable pair, which is exactly the shape a multiple-choice comparison question takes.

topics.description: Reviewing, scheduling, and recording changes before applying them, so that an incident can be correlated with what changed.
topics.notes: Depth rationale: either end of a named confusable pair, which is exactly the shape a multiple-choice comparison question takes.

topics.description: Keeping machines configured alike so that a fix, a script, or a runbook applies everywhere rather than to one snowflake host.
topics.notes: Depth rationale: conceptual: explain what it is and why it exists.

topics.description: Predictable names for hosts, users, and resources, so that identity and purpose can be inferred without a lookup.
topics.notes: Depth rationale: conceptual: explain what it is and why it exists.

topics.description: Scripting repeated work, and writing it so that running it twice is safe and leaves the same result.
topics.notes: Depth rationale: either end of a named confusable pair, which is exactly the shape a multiple-choice comparison question takes.

topics.description: Declaring desired system state in version-controlled files and having a tool enforce it — Ansible, Puppet, Chef, Salt.
topics.notes: Depth rationale: either end of a named confusable pair, which is exactly the shape a multiple-choice comparison question takes.

topics.description: Keeping configuration in Git so changes are reviewable, attributable, and revertible.
topics.notes: Depth rationale: conceptual: explain what it is and why it exists.

topics.description: Validating changes in a non-production environment first, and having a rollback path before you need one.
topics.notes: Depth rationale: conceptual: explain what it is and why it exists.

topics.description: Collecting metrics and logs continuously, and notifying a human when a threshold or condition is breached. Monitoring observes; alerting interrupts.
topics.notes: Depth rationale: either end of a named confusable pair, which is exactly the shape a multiple-choice comparison question takes.

topics.description: Projecting resource growth so that expansion is planned rather than triggered by an outage.
topics.notes: Depth rationale: conceptual: explain what it is and why it exists.

topics.description: Agreed periods for disruptive work, communicated in advance to the people affected.
topics.notes: Depth rationale: conceptual: explain what it is and why it exists.

topics.description: Splitting a sensitive workflow so no single person can both make and approve a change.
topics.notes: Depth rationale: conceptual: explain what it is and why it exists.

topics.description: Step-by-step procedures for known operational tasks and incidents, written to be followed under pressure.
topics.notes: Depth rationale: either end of a named confusable pair, which is exactly the shape a multiple-choice comparison question takes.

topics.description: Maintaining an accurate record of what systems exist, what runs on them, and who owns them. You cannot patch, secure, or decommission what you do not know about.
topics.notes: Depth rationale: conceptual: explain what it is and why it exists.

topics.description: A defined minimum secure configuration applied to every system of a given type, so security does not depend on who built the machine.
topics.notes: Depth rationale: conceptual: explain what it is and why it exists.

topics.description: Defined procedures for granting access on joining and — more importantly — revoking every credential on departure. Orphaned accounts are a standing risk.
topics.notes: Depth rationale: conceptual: explain what it is and why it exists.

topics.description: Capturing a restorable copy or snapshot before a risky change, so rollback does not depend on the change going as planned.
topics.notes: Depth rationale: conceptual: explain what it is and why it exists.

topics.description: A regular, scheduled rhythm for applying updates, with an expedited path for critical security fixes — distinct from the mechanics of patching itself.
topics.notes: Depth rationale: either end of a named confusable pair, which is exactly the shape a multiple-choice comparison question takes.

topics.description: Configuring systems so they behave as an experienced administrator would expect, because surprising setups fail during incidents when nobody has time to read.
topics.notes: Depth rationale: peripheral or specialist for an entry-level exam; recognition of the term is sufficient.

topics.description: Every service having a named owner responsible for its health, cost and lifecycle, so nothing is silently unmaintained.
topics.notes: Depth rationale: peripheral or specialist for an entry-level exam; recognition of the term is sufficient.

topics.description: A seven-layer reference model. Its value for an administrator is as a fault-isolation ladder: establish which layer is broken before touching anything.
topics.notes: Layer numbering and what lives at each layer are commonly tested. Depth rationale: either end of a named confusable pair, which is exactly the shape a multiple-choice comparison question takes.

topics.description: The four-layer model networks are actually built on: link, internet, transport, application.
topics.notes: Depth rationale: either end of a named confusable pair, which is exactly the shape a multiple-choice comparison question takes.

topics.description: A 32-bit address written as four dotted decimal octets, split by the subnet mask into a network portion and a host portion.
topics.notes: Depth rationale: command-bearing: the exam can ask which command or option fits a stated need.

topics.description: A 128-bit address in hexadecimal groups, introduced because IPv4 space was exhausted. Recognition-level for LFCA.
topics.notes: Depth rationale: command-bearing: the exam can ask which command or option fits a stated need.

topics.description: Marks where the network portion of an address ends. /24 and 255.255.255.0 say the same thing in two notations.
topics.notes: Being able to move between dotted-decimal and prefix notation is expected. Depth rationale: command-bearing: the exam can ask which command or option fits a stated need.

topics.description: Within a subnet the lowest address identifies the network and the highest is the broadcast; neither can be assigned to a host.
topics.notes: Depth rationale: either end of a named confusable pair, which is exactly the shape a multiple-choice comparison question takes.

topics.description: RFC 1918 ranges — 10/8, 172.16/12, 192.168/16 — are not routable on the internet and must be translated to reach it.
topics.notes: A named comparison for this exam. Depth rationale: either end of a named confusable pair, which is exactly the shape a multiple-choice comparison question takes.

topics.description: 127.0.0.1, the interface a host uses to talk to itself. Reaching a service on loopback but not from outside localises the fault sharply.
topics.notes: Depth rationale: command-bearing: the exam can ask which command or option fits a stated need.

topics.description: An address configured by hand and permanent, versus one leased from DHCP. Servers usually want static or a DHCP reservation.
topics.notes: Depth rationale: either end of a named confusable pair, which is exactly the shape a multiple-choice comparison question takes.

topics.description: The 48-bit hardware address used within a single link. It does not cross routers, which is the key difference from an IP address.
topics.notes: Depth rationale: command-bearing: the exam can ask which command or option fits a stated need.

topics.description: Resolves an IPv4 address to a MAC address on the local segment — the join between layer 3 and layer 2.
topics.notes: Depth rationale: command-bearing: the exam can ask which command or option fits a stated need.

topics.description: The legacy classful scheme: class A /8, class B /16, class C /24, with class D reserved for multicast. Superseded by CIDR, but the vocabulary persists and is still examined.
topics.notes: Depth rationale: either end of a named confusable pair, which is exactly the shape a multiple-choice comparison question takes.

topics.description: The router a host sends traffic to when the destination is not on its own subnet. A missing or wrong gateway looks like "local works, internet does not".
topics.notes: One of the highest-yield troubleshooting concepts on the exam. Depth rationale: command-bearing: the exam can ask which command or option fits a stated need.

topics.description: The ordered rules a host consults to decide which interface and next hop to use, most specific prefix first.
topics.notes: Depth rationale: command-bearing: the exam can ask which command or option fits a stated need.

topics.description: A switch forwards frames by MAC within one network; a router forwards packets by IP between networks.
topics.notes: A named comparison. Depth rationale: either end of a named confusable pair, which is exactly the shape a multiple-choice comparison question takes.

topics.description: Rewrites private source addresses to a public one so many internal hosts can share it. The reason inbound connections need explicit port forwarding.
topics.notes: Depth rationale: either end of a named confusable pair, which is exactly the shape a multiple-choice comparison question takes.

topics.description: A logical grouping of devices into a separate broadcast domain, independent of physical location; 802.1Q tagging on trunk links lets a single VLAN span multiple switches. Recognition-level.
topics.notes: Corrected in stage 5 against primary documentation (https://standards.ieee.org/ieee/802.1Q/10323/); the correction survived independent adversarial review. Depth rationale: conceptual: explain what it is and why it exists.

topics.description: The distributed system translating names into IP addresses. Very many "the network is down" reports are actually DNS failures.
topics.notes: DNS vs DHCP is a named comparison and a common confusion. Depth rationale: command-bearing: the exam can ask which command or option fits a stated need.

topics.description: A lookup consults /etc/hosts before querying a nameserver, which is why a stale hosts entry can override a correct DNS record.
topics.notes: Depth rationale: command-bearing: the exam can ask which command or option fits a stated need.

topics.description: Lists the nameservers the resolver queries. On modern systems it is often generated rather than hand-edited.
topics.notes: Depth rationale: either end of a named confusable pair, which is exactly the shape a multiple-choice comparison question takes.

topics.description: A local static name-to-address file, consulted before DNS.
topics.notes: Depth rationale: either end of a named confusable pair, which is exactly the shape a multiple-choice comparison question takes.

topics.description: A maps a name to IPv4, AAAA to IPv6, CNAME aliases one name to another, MX directs mail, PTR does reverse lookup, TXT carries arbitrary text such as SPF.
topics.notes: A vs CNAME and the purpose of MX and PTR are commonly tested. Depth rationale: command-bearing: the exam can ask which command or option fits a stated need.

topics.description: A fully qualified domain name locates a host absolutely within the DNS hierarchy; a bare hostname does not.
topics.notes: Depth rationale: command-bearing: the exam can ask which command or option fits a stated need.

topics.description: Records carry a time-to-live governing how long resolvers cache them, which is why a DNS change is not visible everywhere at once.
topics.notes: Depth rationale: command-bearing: the exam can ask which command or option fits a stated need.

topics.description: Automatically issues addressing configuration — address, mask, gateway, DNS servers — to clients, removing per-host manual setup.
topics.notes: DHCP hands out addresses; DNS resolves names. Conflating them is the classic error. Depth rationale: either end of a named confusable pair, which is exactly the shape a multiple-choice comparison question takes.

topics.description: A time-bounded allocation of an address which the client must renew, allowing addresses to be reclaimed.
topics.notes: Depth rationale: conceptual: explain what it is and why it exists.

topics.description: Binds a specific MAC address to a fixed IP, giving stability without configuring the host by hand.
topics.notes: Depth rationale: either end of a named confusable pair, which is exactly the shape a multiple-choice comparison question takes.

topics.description: TCP is connection-oriented, ordered, and retransmits lost data; UDP is connectionless and does none of that, trading reliability for latency.
topics.notes: A named comparison and a near-certain topic. Depth rationale: conceptual: explain what it is and why it exists.

topics.description: SYN, SYN-ACK, ACK — the exchange establishing a TCP connection.
topics.notes: Depth rationale: command-bearing: the exam can ask which command or option fits a stated need.

topics.description: A port identifies a service on a host; combined with the IP address it forms the socket that identifies one end of a connection.
topics.notes: Depth rationale: command-bearing: the exam can ask which command or option fits a stated need.

topics.description: The conventional service assignments an administrator should recognise on sight: 22 SSH, 25 SMTP, 53 DNS, 80 HTTP, 443 HTTPS, 143 IMAP, 3306 MySQL, 5432 PostgreSQL, 3389 RDP. Strictly, only 0-1023 are IANA "well-known"; 3306, 5432 and 3389 are registered ports.
topics.notes: Direct recall of the common assignments is very likely to be tested. Note the terminology trap: "well-known" strictly means 0-1023, so 3306 and 5432 are registered ports, not well-known ones. topics.description: A listening socket waits for clients; an established one is an active conversation. Distinguishing them is central to "is the service actually running?".

topics.description: A hot site is fully equipped with the most recent backup already loaded, needing only the data written since that backup before it can take over — real-time, continuously mirrored data belongs to a separate, more expensive mirrored site, not the hot site tier; a warm site is partially equipped and holds hardware but not current data, which must be restored before it can serve; a cold site has the basic space, power and environmental control only, with no hardware or telecommunications in place. Cost falls and recovery time rises as you move from hot to cold.
